While the eurosystem as a whole is progressing more quickly on climate than many central banks in the G20, the Bundesbank has sometimes been seen as an obstacle to action by the ECB. This may be beginning to change, with the central bank dropping its opposition to greening the eurosystem’s monetary policy operations, and moving to procedure data on companies’ climate impacts. * The Bundesbank procured data on companies’ climate impacts, to be used by eurosystem central banks to green their balance sheets, and to support their regulatory functions. * The Bundesbank has historically opposed climate action by the ECB. ## Price stability and climate change. # Price stability and climate change ECB Conference on Climate and Price Stability: Navigating Inflation and Monetary Policy in the Green Transition. I am sure, we all agree: climate change alters the environment in which central banks operate. According to the NGFS long-term scenarios, unmitigated climate change leads to losses in global GDP of almost 15 % by 2050 – relative to a scenario without climate change. Given the context of this conference, there is no need to give you any further examples about the relevance of climate change. Instead, allow me to briefly recap why and how we as central bankers need to deal with climate change: In doing so, I will focus on some of the most important aspects. Let me turn to the two dimensions of what we call “climate change” for short: the impacts of climate change itself, and the effects of our attempts to mitigate it. This is why I highly appreciate that the impacts of physical risk and transition risk on inflation are at the core of today’s conference. One key finding is that food prices tend to rise in the aftermath of a weather shock – associated with negative supply impacts – with some spillovers into overall inflation. This goes hand in hand with substantial structural changes that can also pose risks for price stability. Depending on the policy mix, the pace of technological progress, changes in preferences and the role of international trade relations – to mention just a few main aspects – the transition will affect the supply and demand side of the economy in multiple ways. Therefore, inflationary pressures are likely to remain contained in the medium to long run, especially in the event of an orderly transition with predictable carbon prices. Along the way, central banks will have to make sure that inflation expectations remain well-anchored, as maintaining price stability is their core mandate. The physical principles of climate change have not changed. Events like this conference are important to keep the attention on the problem and to improve our understanding of climate risks.

results.content: # The role of the Deutsche Bundesbank in the European System of Central Banks. On January 1, 1999 stage three of the European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) began, and the European Central Bank (ECB) assumed responsibility for the single monetary policy in the euro area, the second largest economic area in the world after the U.S. On that date, 11 states transferred their sovereignty with regard to monetary policy to a supranational institution. It starts in Section 2 by describing the given central bank structure in the euro area, which is generally characterised by a centralised decision-making process and a decentralised implementation of these decisions. Section 3 describes the role of the national central banks in the Eurosystem and takes a closer look at the case of the Deutsche Bundesbank. The legal basis for the single monetary policy is the treaty establishing the European Community (EC) which—together with the statute of the European System of Central Banks (ESCB) and of the ECB—established both the ECB and the ESCB as from June 1, 1998. The ESCB comprises the ECB—which is the successor of the European Monetary Institute (EMI)—and the National Central Banks (NCBs) of all 15 European Union (EU) member states (see Fig. 1), which are Austria, Belgium, Finland, France, Germany,. The quintessential field of activity for a central bank is certainly monetary policy. The basic principle governing the division of functions between the ECB and the NCBs is unambiguous: centralised decision-making on the ECB Governing Council and decentralised implementation of monetary policy at the NCBs, with the Executive Board of the ECB being empowered to give the necessary instructions to the NCBs. Therefore, in taking its decisions on the way in which the tasks of the ESCB are to be carried out, the ECB adheres to the principle of decentralisation laid down in the treaty. ### Central bank constitutions for federal monetary unions.
